title: Hans heirathet
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 84. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 84, barely a page long and built on a single pun. A young farmer’s cousin sets Hans behind a well-heated stove with a pot of milk, white bread to crumble into it and a shining new Heller in his fist, then goes to a rich farmer and describes exactly that in words that sound like wealth: the boy sits warm, has a good penny in hand, plenty to crumble in, and no fewer Placken than his cousin — Placken being both a plot of land and a patch on a pair of breeches, which is what he slaps as he says it. The bride is won and never undeceived, and the teller signs off with a mock boast of having been at the wedding in a gown of cobweb and slippers of glass. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (heirathet, gieng, ward).

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein junger Bauer, der hieß Hans, dem wollte sein Vetter gern eine reiche Frau werben.
sentences.l: There was once a young peasant, he was called Hans; for him his cousin wanted gladly to woo a rich wife.
sentences.i: There was once a young farmer called Hans, and his cousin was eager to win him a rich wife.
sentences.n: werben with the dative — “dem wollte sein Vetter … werben” — is to court a woman on another man’s behalf; the Vetter is the go-between. The tale runs two relative clauses on with der and dem where English would start fresh. Vetter is cousin, but in older usage any male kinsman.

sentences.t: Da setzte er den Hans hinter den Ofen und ließ gut einheizen.
sentences.l: Then he set the Hans behind the stove and had it heated well.
sentences.i: So he sat Hans down behind the stove and had a good fire made up.
sentences.n: der Hans with the article is the familiar way of naming a person in these tales; English drops it. lassen + infinitive is to have a thing done; einheizen (separable ein-) is to stoke the stove. The bench behind the tiled stove was the warmest seat in the house — which is what makes the boast “sitzt warm” below literally true.

sentences.t: Dann holte er einen Topf Milch und eine gute Menge Weißbrot, gab ihm einen neugemünzten glänzenden Heller in die Hand und sprach „Hans, den Heller da halt fest und das Weißbrot, das brocke in die Milch, und bleib da sitzen, und geh mir nicht von der Stelle, bis ich wiederkomme.“
sentences.l: Then he fetched a pot of milk and a good quantity of white bread, gave him a newly minted shining Heller in the hand and spoke “Hans, that Heller hold fast, and the white bread, that crumble into the milk, and stay sitting there, and do not go from the spot on me, until I come back.”
sentences.i: Then he fetched a pot of milk and a good quantity of white bread, put a newly minted, shining Heller into his hand and said: “Hans, hold that Heller tight; and the white bread — crumble that into the milk; and stay sitting there, and do not stir from the spot until I come back.”
sentences.n: A Heller was the smallest copper coin, worth next to nothing — the trick turns on its being new and bright. “das Weißbrot, das brocke” puts the object first and then takes it up again with das, a fronting common in speech. “geh mir nicht von der Stelle” has the ethic dative mir, which English can only render as “on me” or drop. Weißbrot is fine wheaten bread, a luxury beside black rye.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach der Hans, „das will ich alles ausrichten.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” spoke the Hans, “that will I all carry out.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Hans, “I shall see to all of it.”
sentences.n: sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen where a modern teller would write sagte; it runs through the whole tale. The object das stands first, so the verb comes second and the subject follows it — German V2 order.

sentences.t: Nun zog der Werber ein paar alte verplackte Hosen an, gieng ins andere Dorf zu einer reichen Bauerntochter und sprach „wollt ihr nicht meinen Vetter Hans heirathen? ihr kriegt einen wackern und gescheidten Mann, der euch gefallen wird.“
sentences.l: Now the wooer put on a pair of old patched trousers, went into the other village to a rich peasant’s-daughter and spoke “will you not marry my cousin Hans? you get a brave and clever man, who will please you.”
sentences.i: Now the matchmaker put on a pair of old patched breeches, went over to the next village to a rich farmer’s daughter and said: “Will you not marry my cousin Hans? You will get a fine, sensible husband, one who will please you.”
sentences.n: verplackt — covered in Placken, patches — is the hinge of the whole tale, because Placken means both a patch on a garment and a plot of land. zog … an is the separable anziehen, its prefix left waiting at the end of the clause. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging, gescheidt of gescheit, heirathen of heiraten. ihr is the polite plural “you” between strangers.

sentences.t: Fragte der geizige Vater „wie siehts aus mit seinem Vermögen? hat er auch was einzubrocken?“
sentences.l: Asked the miserly father “how does it look with his property? has he anything to crumble in as well?”
sentences.i: The miserly father asked: “How does it stand with his property? Has he anything of his own to put in the pot?”
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb — “Fragte der geizige Vater” — a lively narrative inversion; l keeps it, at the cost of sounding abrupt, and i supplies the subject first. “einzubrocken haben” is zu + infinitive of einbrocken, to crumble bread into milk; it means here to have means of one’s own. The father puns without knowing it: bread to crumble in is exactly what Hans has, and nothing else. siehts = sieht es.

sentences.t: „Lieber Freund,“ antwortete der Werber, „mein junger Vetter sitzt warm, hat einen guten schönen Pfennig in der Hand, und hat wohl einzubrocken.
sentences.l: “Dear friend,” answered the wooer, “my young cousin sits warm, has a good fine penny in his hand, and has indeed something to crumble in.
sentences.i: “My dear fellow,” answered the matchmaker, “my young cousin sits warm, has a good fine penny in his hand, and has plenty to crumble in.
sentences.n: Every word is true and every word is meant to be heard as a figure: “warm sitzen” means to be comfortably off (he is sitting behind the stove), and “einen schönen Pfennig in der Hand haben” means to have money (he is holding one Heller). The whole speech works this way.

sentences.t: Er sollte auch nicht weniger Placken (wie man die Güter nannte) zählen, als ich,“ und schlug sich dabei auf seine geplackte Hose.
sentences.l: He should also count no fewer Placken (as the estates were called) than I,” and struck himself thereby on his patched trousers.
sentences.i: He can count no fewer Placken (as the holdings were called) than I can,” — and with that he slapped his patched breeches.
sentences.n: The parenthesis “(wie man die Güter nannte)” is the Grimms’ own explanation set inside the text: Placken was a local word for plots of land, and it is also the word for the patches on his trousers. sollte here is not obligation but the reckoning of a claim — is to be counted as. The slap on the breeches is the proof he offers.

sentences.t: „Wollt ihr euch die Mühe nehmen mit mir hinzugehen, soll euch zur Stunde gezeigt werden daß alles so ist, wie ich sage.“
sentences.l: “Will you take upon yourselves the trouble of going there with me, it shall be shown you within the hour that everything is so as I say.”
sentences.i: “If you will take the trouble to come along with me, you shall be shown within the hour that everything is as I say.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb stands first — “Wollt ihr euch die Mühe nehmen” — and English must supply the “if.” “zur Stunde” = at once, this very hour. “soll … gezeigt werden” is the passive with sollen, the promise of a man striking a bargain. Note that daß takes no comma before it here, as often in 1857 printing.

sentences.t: Da wollte der Geizhals die gute Gelegenheit nicht fahren lassen und sprach „wenn dem so ist, so habe ich weiter nichts gegen die Heirath.“
sentences.l: Then the miser did not want to let the good opportunity go, and spoke “if it is so with it, then I have nothing further against the marriage.”
sentences.i: The skinflint had no mind to let so good an opportunity slip, and said: “If that is how it stands, I have nothing further against the match.”
sentences.n: “fahren lassen” = to let go, let slip. “wenn dem so ist” keeps an old dative dem — if it is so with the matter; the modern phrase is wenn es so ist. Geizhals is literally a greed-throat, a hard old word for a miser. Heirath is the 1857 spelling of Heirat.

sentences.t: Nun ward die Hochzeit an dem bestimmten Tag gefeiert, und als die junge Frau ins Feld gehen und die Güter des Bräutigams sehen wollte, zog Hans erst sein sonntägliches Kleid aus und seinen verplackten Kittel an und sprach „ich könnte mir das gute Kleid verunehren.“
sentences.l: Now the wedding was celebrated on the appointed day, and when the young wife wanted to go into the field and see the bridegroom’s estates, Hans first took off his Sunday clothes and put on his patched smock and spoke “I might dishonour the good clothes.”
sentences.i: Now the wedding was celebrated on the appointed day; and when the young wife wanted to go out into the fields and see the bridegroom’s holdings, Hans first took off his Sunday coat and put on his patched smock, saying: “I might spoil my good clothes.”
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde, and here forms the passive “was celebrated.” The tale sets the two separable verbs side by side with their prefixes stranded at the end — “zog … aus … und … an.” Kleid here is not a dress but a suit of clothes. verunehren = to bring dishonour on, hence to spoil.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie zusammen ins Feld, und wo sich auf dem Weg der Weinstock abzeichnete, oder Äcker und Wiesen abgetheilt waren, deutete Hans mit dem Finger und schlug dann an einen großen oder kleinen Placken seines Kittels, und sprach „der Placken ist mein und jener auch, mein Schatz, schauet nur danach,“
sentences.l: Then they went together into the field, and wherever on the way the vine marked itself out, or fields and meadows were divided off, Hans pointed with his finger and then struck at a large or a small patch of his smock, and spoke “that patch is mine and that one too, my treasure, only look at it,”
sentences.i: So they went out together into the fields; and wherever the vine stood out along the way, or ploughland and meadow were marked off from one another, Hans pointed with his finger and then slapped a large or a small patch of his smock, saying: “That plot is mine, and that one too, my dear — only look at it,”
sentences.n: The joke stands wholly on Placken meaning both the patch on his smock and a plot of ground, so that what he points at and what he slaps are one word. “sich abzeichnen” = to stand out, show up against its surroundings. abgetheilt is the 1857 spelling of abgeteilt. schauet is the old plural imperative — he is still saying ihr to his own wife on the wedding journey.

sentences.t: und wollte damit sagen, die Frau sollte nicht in das weite Feld gaffen, sondern auf sein Kleid schauen, das wäre sein eigen.
sentences.l: and he wanted to say by that, the wife should not gape into the wide field, but look at his clothes — that was his own.
sentences.i: and what he meant by it was that his wife should not be gaping out over the broad fields, but looking at his coat: that was what was his own.
sentences.n: sollte and wäre are subjunctives of reported speech: the tale is giving his thought, not making the statement itself, and English marks it with “should” and with the reporting frame. gaffen is to stare open-mouthed, a coarser word set against schauen in the same sentence. “sein eigen” = his own property.

sentences.t: „Bist du auch auf der Hochzeit gewesen?“
sentences.l: “Have you been at the wedding too?”
sentences.i: “And were you at the wedding as well?”
sentences.n: The tale closes with the teller handing the story back to the listeners in a mock exchange. German uses the perfect “bist du gewesen” where English prefers the simple past.

sentences.t: „Ja wohl bin ich darauf gewesen, und in vollem Staat.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed I have been at it, and in full state.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed I was, and in full finery.
sentences.n: “in vollem Staat” = in full dress, in all one’s finery; Staat in this old sense is show and display, not the state. darauf = at it, upon it, pointing back to the wedding.

sentences.t: Mein Kopfputz war von Schnee, da kam die Sonne, und er ist mir abgeschmolzen;
sentences.l: My head-dress was of snow, then came the sun, and it has melted off me;
sentences.i: My headdress was of snow — then the sun came, and it melted away on me;
sentences.n: These three boasts are the standard nonsense-ending: everything worn was made of something that cannot last. “ist mir abgeschmolzen” puts the person in the dative — melted off me — and takes sein in the perfect, as verbs of change of state do. Kopfputz is the elaborate headgear of a peasant woman’s festival dress.

sentences.t: mein Kleid war von Spinneweb, da kam ich durch Dornen, die rissen mir es ab;
sentences.l: my clothes were of spider-web, then I came through thorns, they tore it off me;
sentences.i: my gown was of cobweb — then I came through thorns, and they tore it off me;
sentences.n: die is a demonstrative here, “those, they,” taking up Dornen where modern German would simply repeat sie. “rissen mir es ab” again sets the person in the dative: tore it off me; abreißen is separable.

sentences.t: meine Pantoffel waren von Glas, da stieß ich an einen Stein, da sagten sie klink! und sprangen entzwei.“
sentences.l: my slippers were of glass, then I struck against a stone, then they said clink! and sprang in two.”
sentences.i: my slippers were of glass — then I knocked against a stone, and they said clink! and sprang in two.”
sentences.n: klink is the sound itself standing where a verb would; it is the same word as the click of a door-latch. “sprangen entzwei” = sprang apart in two, shattered. Pantoffel here is the old plural without an ending.

glossary.fahren: fahren — to travel, go; in fahren lassen: to let go, let slip
glossary.gefallen: gefallen — to please (+ dative: der euch gefallen wird, who will please you)
glossary.halt: halten — hold! (imperative sg.; halt fest = hold tight, not the interjection halt!)
glossary.heller: der Heller — heller, the smallest copper coin, worth next to nothing (not the adjective hell, bright)
glossary.kleid: das Kleid — here a suit of clothes, a garment, not specifically a dress
glossary.sage: sagen — (I) say (1 sg. present, wie ich sage: as I say)
glossary.schatz: der Schatz — treasure; as a form of address, sweetheart, my dear
glossary.setzte: setzen — set, placed (3 sg. past, transitive: setzte er den Hans hinter den Ofen)
glossary.staat: der Staat — show, display, finery (in vollem Staat: in full dress; the old sense, not the state)
